summary: Westmorland sits on the dead-flat floor of the Imperial Valley, roughly fifteen feet below sea level, where the Salton Sea shimmers to the north and open agricultural fields stretch to every horizon — a landscape so level that sunset light sweeps unbroken across irrigated rows of alfalfa, sugar beets, and winter vegetables for what feels like minutes longer than anywhere else in California. At just 0.6 square miles, the entire town is walkable end to end, but there is almost nothing commercial to walk to; this is a place shaped almost entirely by Imperial Valley agriculture, with farming and related logistics providing the bulk of local employment. The affordability numbers look striking at first — a median home value around $218,600 — until you set it against a median household income under $29,000, producing a price-to-income ratio above 7.5, which makes homeownership a genuine stretch even at these relatively low sticker prices. Nearly half the population lives below the poverty line, and rent averaging $817 per month consumes a significant share of local earnings. Summer highs routinely push well past 100°F, with an annual average daytime temperature of 89°F and nearly eleven hours of sunshine daily — air conditioning isn't optional, it's survival infrastructure. Westmorland is, in essence, a tiny agricultural node where the cost of living looks low on paper but lands hard against the incomes the local economy actually generates.
